quests.hint: Notice the short, crisp 's' sound at the end of 'cooks'.
quests.explanation: We add -s to the verb after he, she, or it in the present simple, so it's 'cooks', not 'cook'. This tense is used for daily habits and routines.
quests.textToSpeak: My father cooks dinner every evening.
quests.correctAnswer: My father cooks dinner every evening.

quests.hint: Let 'sleeps' and 'under' flow together without a pause.
quests.explanation: 'Under' is a preposition of place that tells us exactly where the cat sleeps. Prepositions like this are key to describing locations in English.
quests.textToSpeak: The cat sleeps under my bed.
quests.correctAnswer: The cat sleeps under my bed.

quests.hint: Say 'for lunch' as one smooth beat, not two separate words.
quests.explanation: 'For' often pairs with meals, as in 'for breakfast' or 'for dinner'. Learning these small word partnerships helps you sound more natural.
quests.textToSpeak: We eat rice for lunch today.
quests.correctAnswer: We eat rice for lunch today.

quests.hint: 'Orange juice' carries stress on both words: ORANGE JUICE.
quests.explanation: When two nouns combine like this, both usually keep clear stress. 'Orange juice' is one of the most common breakfast phrases in English.
quests.textToSpeak: She drinks orange juice every morning.
quests.correctAnswer: She drinks orange juice every morning.

quests.hint: The word 'before' signals what happens first, so say it clearly.
quests.explanation: 'Before' connects two actions in time order. Time words like this help listeners understand the sequence of events in a sentence.
quests.textToSpeak: I wash my hands before eating.
quests.correctAnswer: I wash my hands before eating.

quests.hint: Colour words like 'blue' usually get a little extra stress.
quests.explanation: In English, colour adjectives come directly before the noun: 'a blue shirt', not 'a shirt blue'. Word order matters for clear meaning.
quests.textToSpeak: He wears a blue shirt today.
quests.correctAnswer: He wears a blue shirt today.

quests.hint: Notice the 'z' sound in 'waters' — it isn't an 's' sound.
quests.explanation: The verb 'waters' takes the -s ending for he/she/it, and here it's pronounced /z/, not /s/. Small sound shifts like this are common in English.
quests.textToSpeak: My mum waters the plants every day.
quests.correctAnswer: My mum waters the plants every day.

quests.hint: Link 'play' and 'football' smoothly, almost like one word.
quests.explanation: 'Play' is used with sports and games, as in 'play football' or 'play tennis'. This is a fixed pairing you'll hear constantly in everyday English.
quests.textToSpeak: They play football in the park.
quests.correctAnswer: They play football in the park.

quests.hint: Stress falls on the first syllable: CRIES.
quests.explanation: 'During' introduces a period of time when something happens. It's a very useful word for describing when events take place.
quests.textToSpeak: The baby cries during the night.
quests.correctAnswer: The baby cries during the night.

quests.hint: 'Whiteboard' is one word with the stress on WHITE.
quests.explanation: Compound nouns like 'whiteboard' usually stress the first part. Classroom vocabulary like this comes up often in everyday conversation about school.
quests.textToSpeak: Our teacher writes on the whiteboard.
quests.correctAnswer: Our teacher writes on the whiteboard.

quests.hint: 'Twice a day' is a fixed phrase — keep it flowing as one unit.
quests.explanation: 'Twice' means two times, just as 'once' means one time. These frequency words are essential for talking about daily routines.
quests.textToSpeak: I brush my teeth twice a day.
quests.correctAnswer: I brush my teeth twice a day.

quests.hint: Say the final 's' in 'feeds' clearly to show the present tense.
quests.explanation: 'Feeds' shows the present simple for a routine action. 'After school' is a common time phrase for describing what happens once classes end.
quests.textToSpeak: She feeds the dog after school.
quests.correctAnswer: She feeds the dog after school.

quests.hint: 'TV' is said as two separate letters: TEE-VEE.
quests.explanation: 'TV' is an abbreviation pronounced letter by letter, unlike most English words. Many common nouns are shortened this way in everyday speech.
quests.textToSpeak: We watch TV after dinner.
quests.correctAnswer: We watch TV after dinner.

quests.hint: Notice the long 'i' sound in 'drives': dr-EYE-vz.
quests.explanation: 'Drives' combines the verb 'drive' with the -s ending for he/she/it. 'Drive to work' is a very common phrase for describing a daily commute.
quests.textToSpeak: He drives his car to work.
quests.correctAnswer: He drives his car to work.

quests.hint: The 'ng' sound in 'sings' comes from the back of your throat.
quests.explanation: 'Sings' ends in the /ŋ/ sound, written as 'ng'. This sound doesn't exist in every language, so it's worth practising carefully.
quests.textToSpeak: My sister sings in the shower.
quests.correctAnswer: My sister sings in the shower.

quests.hint: 'Children' is already plural, so never add an extra 's'.
quests.explanation: 'Children' is an irregular plural noun; the singular is 'child'. Irregular plurals like this simply need to be memorised.
quests.textToSpeak: The children run around the garden.
quests.correctAnswer: The children run around the garden.

quests.hint: In this sentence, 'read' rhymes with 'red', not 'reed'.
quests.explanation: 'Read' is pronounced differently depending on tense: present tense rhymes with 'reed', past tense rhymes with 'red'. Context tells you which one to use.
quests.textToSpeak: I read a book before bed.
quests.correctAnswer: I read a book before bed.

quests.hint: Stress the day of the week clearly: FRI-day.
quests.explanation: Days of the week always start with a capital letter in writing and usually carry sentence stress in speech, since they give key information.
quests.textToSpeak: She cooks pasta every Friday.
quests.correctAnswer: She cooks pasta every Friday.

quests.hint: 'On Sundays' uses the small word 'on' for days of the week.
quests.explanation: English uses 'on' with days ('on Sunday'), 'in' with months ('in May'), and 'at' with clock times ('at six'). These small words follow clear patterns.
quests.textToSpeak: We visit our grandma on Sundays.
quests.correctAnswer: We visit our grandma on Sundays.

quests.hint: Link 'rides his' smoothly — the 's' connects into the 'h' sound.
quests.explanation: 'Rides' pairs naturally with 'bike', just as 'drives' pairs with 'car'. Matching the right verb to the right vehicle is useful everyday vocabulary.
quests.textToSpeak: He rides his bike to school.
quests.correctAnswer: He rides his bike to school.

quests.hint: 'Brightly' ends in a soft '-ly' sound.
quests.explanation: Adding -ly to an adjective often creates an adverb: 'bright' becomes 'brightly'. Adverbs like this describe how an action happens.
quests.textToSpeak: The sun shines brightly today.
quests.correctAnswer: The sun shines brightly today.

quests.hint: 'A lot' sounds like one word: uh-LOT.
quests.explanation: 'A lot' means 'a great amount' and is one of the most common phrases for describing quantity in everyday spoken English.
quests.textToSpeak: It rains a lot in April.
quests.correctAnswer: It rains a lot in April.

quests.hint: 'It's' is a contraction — say it quickly as one syllable.
quests.explanation: 'It's' is short for 'it is'. Contractions like this appear constantly in natural spoken English, so getting comfortable with them really matters.
quests.textToSpeak: I wear a coat when it's cold.
quests.correctAnswer: I wear a coat when it's cold.

quests.hint: 'Umbrella' has stress on the middle syllable: um-BREL-la.
quests.explanation: 'Carries' shows the present simple with -ies, since the verb 'carry' ends in a consonant plus y. This spelling pattern applies to many common verbs.
quests.textToSpeak: She carries an umbrella today.
quests.correctAnswer: She carries an umbrella today.

quests.hint: 'Bakery' has three syllables: BAKE-uh-ree.
quests.explanation: 'Bakery' is the shop, while 'baker' is the person who works there. Shop-name vocabulary like this is useful for talking about daily errands.
quests.textToSpeak: We buy bread from the bakery.
quests.correctAnswer: We buy bread from the bakery.

quests.hint: 'Pays for' needs that small word 'for' before the item.
quests.explanation: In English, we 'pay for' something, always including 'for' before the object. Leaving it out is a very common mistake for learners.
quests.textToSpeak: He pays for the bus tickets.
quests.correctAnswer: He pays for the bus tickets.

quests.hint: 'More than' is the key comparing phrase — say both words clearly.
quests.explanation: 'More than' is used to compare preferences or amounts. This simple structure lets you express opinions and choices in everyday conversation.
quests.textToSpeak: I like apples more than bananas.
quests.correctAnswer: I like apples more than bananas.

quests.hint: 'Has' ends with a /z/ sound here, like 'hazz'.
quests.explanation: 'Has' is the he/she/it form of 'have', used to talk about family members and possessions. It's one of the most frequent verbs in English.
quests.textToSpeak: She has two brothers and a sister.
quests.correctAnswer: She has two brothers and a sister.

quests.hint: 'Next door' is a fixed phrase for the closest neighbouring house.
quests.explanation: 'Next door' describes a nearby location without needing extra words like 'house' or 'flat'. Phrases like this make your English sound more natural.
quests.textToSpeak: My best friend lives next door.
quests.correctAnswer: My best friend lives next door.

quests.hint: 'Celebrate' has stress on the second syllable: ce-LE-brate.
quests.explanation: 'Celebrate' is used for happy occasions like birthdays and holidays. Getting the stress on the right syllable makes the word much easier to understand.
quests.textToSpeak: We celebrate birthdays with chocolate cake.
quests.correctAnswer: We celebrate birthdays with chocolate cake.
